magnus, magna, magnum

adjective; comparative major, superlative maximus

big, large, great

The general word for size, amount and degree: big, large and great alike. Major is “bigger” and also “older”; majōrēs are ancestors (see major).

Other words

  • grandis, grande — big, full-grown, large

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.131: meliōrēs fētūs … et grandiōrēs (Lewis & Short); Cic. Sen. 63: grandis nātū

    Not the everyday word for big (that is magnus), though it can mean it: big as things grow big, vegetables, logs, children, and so full-grown; grandis nātū is “old” (Cic. Sen. 63). It also means great, powerful and, of style, lofty (Lewis & Short).

  • amplus, ampla, amplum — large, of great extent

    also used · classical · Traupman 202

    Of size and extent, often of places and buildings; Traupman’s word for “big” in the geography chapter.

Examples

  • Māla ad crustum, nōn mollia sed dūra, nōn parva sed grandia, emenda erant

    Apples had to be bought for the pie, not soft but firm, not small but bigLibellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis

  • stercilīnum magnum studē ut habeās.

    make sure you have a big manure heap.Cato Agr. 5.8

  • aspice quam tumeat magnō jecur ānsere majus!

    look how it swells, a liver bigger than a big goose!Mart. 13.58.1

See also small, tiny, major, too big, so big!, when you’re big.
